bibliography.abstract: ABSTRACT This study aims to evaluate the impact of Apparent Temperature (AT), a biometeorological index that estimates perceived thermal sensation, on occupational accidents in five Spanish provinces, while separately analyzing accidents in the primary sector (agriculture, forestry, livestock farming, and aquaculture) and construction. An ecological time-series study was conducted over a 17-year period. A Generalized Additive Model combined with a Distributed Lag Non-linear Model using a quasi-Poisson distribution was applied to estimate the association between daily occupational accidents and AT. In the two southern provinces, occupational accidents increase as temperature rises. In contrast, in Ávila, Cantabria, and Pontevedra, the relative risk (RR) of occupational accidents increases at thermal extremes (both low and high AT), although the effect is statistically significant only at low temperatures. In the primary sector, accidents in Cantabria and Pontevedra (the two northern coastal provinces) increase with AT. In Cantabria, the maximum number of accidents occurs at 34°C, where the risk is 1.73 times higher than at 14°C (the AT associated with the minimum number of occupational accidents [ATma]). In Pontevedra, the maximum is reached at 38°C, with a risk 1.48 times higher than at 19°C (ATma). Occupational accidents in construction are statistically significantly associated with AT only in Seville, reaching the highest risk at 40°C, where the risk is 1.38 times higher than at 21°C (ATma). The pattern of association between AT and workplace accidents varies across provinces, which may be influenced by climatic characteristics that, in turn, determine the type of professional activity carried out at different times of the year.

en.caveats: The study relies on an ecological time-series design, which analyzes aggregate provincial data rather than individual-level exposure and circumstances.
en.what: This ecological time-series study analyzed the relationship between daily occupational accidents and Apparent Temperature (AT) over a 17-year period across five Spanish provinces, focusing on the primary and construction sectors. Using a Generalized Additive Model combined with a Distributed Lag Non-linear Model, the researchers found that occupational accidents in the primary sector increase with AT in northern coastal provinces, peaking at 34°C in Cantabria (RR 1.73) and 38°C in Pontevedra (RR 1.48). In construction, a statistically significant association was found only in Seville, where the risk of accidents peaks at 40°C (RR 1.38).
en.why: The study demonstrates that the relationship between thermal stress and workplace accidents is highly localized and sector-specific, showing that northern agricultural workers face elevated risk at high temperatures while southern construction workers are highly vulnerable to extreme heat.
